section.title: Sin, Confession, and the Redeemer
section.sectionRationale: This chapter diagnoses exactly why salvation seemed delayed, not because God's arm was too short, but because sin had built a wall between the people and their God. It moves through unflinching confession into one of Isaiah's most striking images, God Himself, seeing no one to intercede, putting on His own armor of righteousness and salvation to act alone.
section.thesis: Israel's sin, not any weakness in God, has separated her from His help, and when God finds no human intercessor able to bring justice, He Himself acts, arming Himself with righteousness and salvation to come as Redeemer to those in Jacob who turn from transgression.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the LORD's hand is not too short to save; a raw confession of sin's true shape; the LORD sees no one to intercede and acts Himself; and the covenant promise, My Spirit and My words will never depart from you.

verses.text: Surely the arm of the LORD is not too short to save, nor His ear too dull to hear.
But your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you, so that He does not hear.
For your hands are stained with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies, and your tongue mutters injustice.

units.label: They hatch the eggs of vipers
units.note: a raw confession of sin's shape

verses.text: No one calls for justice; no one pleads his case honestly. They rely on empty pleas; they tell lies; they conceive mischief and give birth to iniquity.
They hatch the eggs of vipers and weave a spider’s web. Whoever eats their eggs will die; crack one open, and a viper is hatched.
Their cobwebs cannot be made into clothing, and they cannot cover themselves with their works. Their deeds are sinful deeds, and acts of violence are in their hands.
Their feet run to evil; they are swift to shed innocent blood. Their thoughts are sinful thoughts; ruin and destruction lie in their wake.
The way of peace they have not known, and there is no justice in their tracks. They have turned them into crooked paths; no one who treads on them will know peace.
Therefore justice is far from us, and righteousness does not reach us. We hope for light, but there is darkness; for brightness, but we walk in gloom.
Like the blind, we feel our way along the wall, groping like those without eyes. We stumble at midday as in the twilight; among the vigorous we are like the dead.
We all growl like bears and moan like doves. We hope for justice, but find none, for salvation, but it is far from us.
For our transgressions are multiplied before You, and our sins testify against us. Our transgressions are indeed with us, and we know our iniquities:
rebelling and denying the LORD, turning away from our God, speaking oppression and revolt, conceiving and uttering lies from the heart.
So justice is turned away, and righteousness stands at a distance. For truth has stumbled in the public square, and honesty cannot enter.
Truth is missing, and whoever turns from evil becomes prey. The LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice.

units.label: His own arm brought Him salvation
units.note: the armor of righteousness and salvation

verses.text: He saw that there was no man; He was amazed that there was no one to {{paga|intercede}}. So His own arm brought salvation, and His own righteousness sustained Him.
He put on righteousness like a breastplate, and the helmet of salvation on His head; He put on garments of vengeance and wrapped Himself in a cloak of zeal.
So He will repay according to their deeds: fury to His enemies, retribution to His foes, and recompense to the islands.
So shall they fear the name of the LORD where the sun sets, and His glory where it rises. For He will come like a raging flood, driven by the breath of the LORD.

units.label: The Redeemer will come to Zion
units.note: My Spirit, My words, will not depart

verses.text: “The {{goel|Redeemer}} will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression, ” declares the LORD.

“As for Me, this is My covenant with them,” says the LORD. “My Spirit will not depart from you, and My words that I have put in your mouth will not depart from your mouth or from the mouths of your children and grandchildren, from now on and forevermore,” says the LORD.

paga.gloss: To intercede, to meet or intervene on behalf of another. God is amazed to find no one able to paga, intercede, so He acts Himself; the same root describes the LORD laying the iniquity of all upon the Servant in 53:6 and the Servant making intercession for transgressors in 53:12, tying this chapter's crisis directly to its answer.

goel.gloss: Redeemer, kinsman-deliverer, obligated by covenant bond to rescue and restore. Paul quotes this exact verse, the Deliverer will come from Zion, in Romans 11:26, applying it to the future salvation of Israel through Christ, the ultimate go'el who comes to those who turn from transgression.

basic.context: The chapter answers a real question: why has God's salvation not come? Not because His power failed, but because sin built a wall between the people and Him. After a devastatingly honest confession of what that sin actually looks like, lies, violence, no justice, God Himself steps in, finding no human able to intercede, and acts alone, armed for battle.
basic.hermeneutics: The confession in the middle of this chapter is corporate and unflinching, we all growl like bears, our transgressions testify against us, refusing any excuse. The turn in verse 16, God seeing no intercessor and acting Himself, is the theological hinge of the whole passage, salvation must originate entirely with God because no human mediator could be found sufficient.
basic.originalLanguages: God is amazed that there is no one to paga, intercede, so His own arm acts. And the goel, Redeemer, promised to come to Zion in verse 20 is quoted by Paul directly of Christ's future salvation for Israel, Romans 11:26.
basic.typology: God's own armor, righteousness as breastplate, salvation as helmet, anticipates Paul's armor of God in Ephesians 6:14-17, where believers are told to put on the very armor God wears here. The absence of a human intercessor anticipates and is answered by Christ, the one true Intercessor.
basic.christ: Paul quotes verse 20 directly in Romans 11:26, the Deliverer will come from Zion, applying it to Christ's coming salvation for Israel. And where this chapter says God found no one to intercede, Hebrews 7:25 answers that Christ always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through Him, the very lack this chapter mourns, filled.
basic.god: God does not excuse His people's sin, He names it in devastating detail, yet His justice does not leave Him passive; when no human mediator can be found, He Himself supplies both the righteousness and the salvation required, armed and moving toward Zion as Redeemer.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 11:26 quotes verse 20 directly of Christ's future salvation for Israel. Ephesians 6:14-17 has believers wear the same armor of righteousness and salvation God wears here. Hebrews 7:25 answers this chapter's missing intercessor with Christ, who always lives to intercede.
basic.oneStory: Sin always separates, and no human effort or mediator proves sufficient to close that gap; that is the honest diagnosis of this chapter. Its answer, God Himself acting, coming as armed Redeemer, is fulfilled in Christ, both the Deliverer Paul says will come from Zion and the great High Priest who intercedes exactly where this chapter found no one able to.

context.literary:
Isaiah 59 is built on a shifting set of pronouns, and the shifts are the argument. Verses 1 to 2 address a 'you' and open with a charge. Verses 3 to 8 describe a 'they', a hard portrait of wrongdoers seen from outside. Then in verses 9 to 15 the speaker slides into 'we' and 'us', and the portrait becomes a confession the prophet shares in rather than merely announces. From the second half of verse 15 the subject is 'He', God looking, being displeased, arming and coming. Verse 21 closes in the first person of God, 'As for Me', a covenant sworn directly to the people. The movement is accusation, description, confession, rescue, covenant.

The middle section is full of paired images. Verses 5 and 6 set the viper's egg against the spider's web, deadly and useless at once, so that what they make is both poison and cobweb, and cannot be worn as clothing. Verses 9 and 10 turn to light and darkness, midday and twilight, the seeing and the blind. Verse 14 gives a courtroom picture: justice is turned back, righteousness stands at a distance, truth has stumbled in the public square and honesty cannot enter, as though the city gate where cases were heard had become unusable.

The garments of verse 6 also set up verse 17. Their works cannot clothe them, but God dresses Himself in righteousness and salvation, so the chapter contrasts two wardrobes. The chapter also reads as the dark mirror of chapter 58, where the promise 'Then your light will break forth like the dawn' hung on repentance, Isaiah 58:8. Chapter 59 shows what happened when the condition was not met: 'We hope for light, but there is darkness,' verse 9. It then prepares the way for chapter 60, where the light finally rises, and the opening 'Arise, shine, for your light has come' in Isaiah 60:1 answers the gloom of 59:9 directly.
context.historical:
The oracles of Isaiah 56 to 66 speak to a community that has seen the exile end or is close to seeing it end, and that finds the promised glory of chapters 40 to 55 slow to arrive. Scholars differ on the exact setting, some placing these chapters among the returned community in Judah and others holding that Isaiah the prophet anticipated that later situation, but the pastoral problem is plain in the text itself. Hopes had been raised and not met, and a bruised people were ready to conclude that the LORD had lost interest or strength.

Isaiah answers with the language Israel had heard before. 'Is the LORD's arm too short?' is the question God put to Moses in the wilderness when the people doubted He could feed them, Numbers 11:23. Here the prophet gives the reply from the other side: the arm is not short, the ear is not dull, the problem is moral. The sins listed are social and civic as much as private: blood on the hands, lying lips, false pleading in court, violence, and a legal system in which truth stumbles in the public square, verse 14. The city gate was the place where elders heard cases, so verse 14 describes a failure of the very institution meant to protect the weak, and verse 15 observes that anyone who turns from evil becomes prey.

Verses 16 to 19 draw on the image of a warrior king. In the ancient world a champion was expected to arm himself and fight for his people, and Israel had known the arm of the LORD in the exodus, Isaiah 51:9. Verse 19 reaches to the west and the east, to the islands and the rising of the sun, which tells the first hearers that this rescue is no local skirmish. Rescue of Zion becomes visible to the whole earth, and the nations that watched Israel's humiliation will fear the name of the LORD.
context.canonical:
The reading of this chapter in Scripture's long story begins with Moses and Ezekiel. Ezekiel 22:30 records the same search: 'I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land, so that I should not destroy it. But I found no one.' Psalm 106:23 remembers the time such a man was found, when Moses stood before Him in the breach and turned away His wrath. Isaiah 59:16 states the sorrow of the opposite case. The earlier Moses could stand in the gap; for this generation there is no one, and so God acts alone.

Isaiah himself links the chapter to its neighbours. The arm of the LORD that awakens in Isaiah 51:9 and is bared in Isaiah 52:10 is the arm that brings salvation here, and the Servant of Isaiah 53:12 is the one who 'made intercession for the transgressors', exactly the work that 59:16 found missing. A little later, Isaiah 63:3 and 63:5 repeat the language of verse 16: 'no one from the nations was with Me,' 'I looked, but there was no one to help.' The warrior who comes in this chapter is the same figure whose garments are stained in chapter 63.

In the New Testament the confession of verses 7 and 8 is gathered into Paul's catalogue of universal sin, 'Their feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery lie in their wake, and the way of peace they have not known,' Romans 3:15-17. Paul draws the whole chapter into his argument that all stand guilty. Isaiah 59:20 and 21 are then quoted and echoed in Romans 11:26-27, where the covenant promise of verse 21 is joined to the taking away of sins. The armour of verse 17 is taken up by Paul in Ephesians 6:14-17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8, and the Spirit and words that never depart from the mouth of the people anticipate the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:33-34.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted a discouraged people to stop asking the wrong question. They were asking why God would not save; he asks them to look at their own hands. By saying that sin has 'built barriers' and 'hidden His face' he places the distance on their side, and by listing the sins in concrete detail, hands, fingers, lips, tongue, feet, thoughts, he refuses a vague confession. Every part of the body is named, so that no part of the person can claim innocence.

He also wanted the confession of verses 9 to 15 to become theirs. The speaker moves from 'they' to 'we', and the shift invites hearers to say the words with him rather than watch someone else do wrong. Honest speech of that kind is itself the beginning of the turning that verse 20 names, since the Redeemer comes to 'those in Jacob who turn from transgression'.

The last purpose is to sustain hope after the confession. God is not silent while His people wake up to their condition. He sees, He is displeased, He is amazed at the absence of anyone able to intercede, and then He moves, arming Himself and coming. The chapter ends not with the people's achievement but with a covenant sworn in the first person, and with the promise that His Spirit and His words will stay with them and with their children and grandchildren. Israel was meant to learn that its security rests on what God has promised and not on its own ability to repent well.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter is description. Verses 3 to 8 report what the community is like, and verses 9 to 15 report how they feel in the dark. None of this is commanded, and none of it should be copied. The confession does give a pattern, however. It does not minimise sin, it does not blame circumstances, and it does not stop at feeling bad: 'we know our iniquities,' verse 12. It names rebellion, denial of the LORD, oppression and lying. A reader who prays this way is doing what the chapter models.

The divine warrior verses need care. God puts on garments of vengeance and speaks of repaying according to deeds, verse 18. That is a statement of what God will do, not a licence for believers to take vengeance. Paul draws the opposite conclusion from Scripture's teaching on divine vengeance in Romans 12:19, leaving it with God. When Ephesians 6 borrows the breastplate and helmet, it is careful to say that the struggle is not against flesh and blood, Ephesians 6:12. The chapter is therefore a call to confess honestly and to wait on the LORD who acts, not a pattern for religious violence.

debates.question: Who is the 'Redeemer' who comes to Zion in verse 20, and what does Paul do with the verse in Romans 11:26?

views.label: God Himself, fulfilled in Christ's first coming
views.case: The warrior of verses 16 to 19 is the LORD, and the Redeemer of verse 20 is the same figure, so the verse speaks of God coming in person. The New Testament reads that coming as the incarnation and the cross, which removes sin from those who turn. On this view Paul quotes the verse because Christ has already come to Zion in the Gospels, and 'all Israel' in Romans 11:26 means the whole people of God drawn from Jew and Gentile.

views.label: Christ at His return, with a future turning of Israel
views.case: Paul writes in the future tense, 'The Deliverer will come from Zion,' and sets it after the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, Romans 11:25-26. Many readers take this to mean a coming still ahead, when a large part of Israel will turn to the Lord. They point out that the Hebrew says the Redeemer comes 'to Zion', while Paul writes 'from Zion', and take the difference to be Paul's deliberate adaptation of the promise.

views.label: An ongoing work through the gospel
views.case: Others hold that the promise is being fulfilled across the age as the gospel goes out from Zion, Isaiah 2:3, and Jews and Gentiles alike turn from transgression. In this reading there is no separate event, only the continuing coming of the Redeemer through the word and Spirit.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on what the verse says about the Redeemer: He is the LORD, He comes for those who turn from transgression, and He brings the covenant of verse 21, in which sin is taken away and the Spirit stays. Where they differ is on timing and on who 'all Israel' is, and that question is better settled by reading Romans 9 to 11 as a whole than by this verse alone.

debates.question: Why does God say He was amazed that there was no one to intercede, when He knows everything?

views.label: A figure of speech for real moral disappointment
views.case: The language belongs to a story told about God in human terms. Elsewhere Scripture shows God asking questions He knows the answer to, as in Genesis 3:9. Here His astonishment expresses how great the gap is between what justice requires and what any human could provide.

views.label: A statement that no human mediator could ever be enough
views.case: Verse 16 is not complaining that someone was slow to volunteer. Nobody in this generation had the righteousness required to stand in the breach, as Moses had in Psalm 106:23. So God supplies what was missing from His own resources: 'His own arm brought salvation, and His own righteousness sustained Him.'

views.label: A foretelling of a mediator who is both God and man
views.case: Christian readers see the missing intercessor answered in Christ, who is God acting in person and also the one mediator between God and men, 1 Timothy 2:5. The rescue is divine, yet it is carried out through a human life and death.

debates.bearing: The three readings are less rivals than layers. The verse shows that deliverance had to come from God, and the New Testament shows how He did it, by becoming the intercessor Himself.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to look at is in verse 2, where the iniquities 'have built barriers' between the people and God. The verb is a form of badal, the root used for separation in Genesis 1:4, 'God separated the light from the darkness,' and Genesis 1:6. It is the verb of creation, the way God divides things so that order appears. Here sin does the dividing, and it sets a separation between the people and the One they depend on. The chapter then plays with the idea of light and darkness in verses 9 to 10, so that the creation vocabulary of the opening chapter is turned on its head: the people live in the dark that sin has made.

Verse 1 borrows a question from the wilderness. The adjective for 'too short' is built on the verb qatsar, and the same wording appears when God asks Moses whether His hand has become short, Numbers 11:23. The idiom links the arm of the LORD to His power to act. Isaiah then uses the arm as a thread through the rest of the chapter: the arm is not short in verse 1, and in verse 16 'His own arm brought salvation.' The same word for arm runs through Isaiah 40:10, 51:9, 52:10 and 53:1, so a reader with the whole scroll in mind hears a long expectation arriving.

In verse 16, the word 'intercede' is the Hebrew paga, with a range from meeting and encountering to striking and falling upon. It is the same root that closes the Servant Song, where the Servant 'made intercession for the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12. In Jeremiah 7:16 God tells the prophet 'do not beg Me', using a form of the same verb for pleading with God. Verse 16 therefore speaks of someone who would step between God and the guilty and press their case. The word is not a technical priestly term. It describes the act of meeting God on another's behalf.

The armour of verse 17 is given in four items, with righteousness (tsedaqah) as the breastplate and salvation (yeshuah) as the helmet. The garments of vengeance and the cloak of zeal complete the dress. The cloak, from the root of the word translated zeal, carries the sense of passionate jealousy for what is God's own, the same word used of the LORD's zeal in Isaiah 9:7. The pairing of righteousness and salvation also matches the pair of what the people lacked in verse 9, 'justice' and 'righteousness'. God supplies in Himself the very things they could not find.

In verse 20 the word goel is the Redeemer, from the family of the kinsman who recovers what has been lost, Leviticus 25:25. Ruth 4 shows him in action, and Isaiah has used the title repeatedly of the LORD, for example in Isaiah 54:5. The Redeemer comes 'to those in Jacob who turn from transgression', where the verb for turn is shuv, the common Hebrew word for repentance, and 'transgression' is pesha, rebellion. The rescue is tied to repentance, which is why the confession of verses 12 to 13 has the same vocabulary: 'rebelling and denying the LORD, turning away from our God.' Finally, in verse 21, 'My Spirit' and 'My words' are set side by side with the covenant, and the same word for Spirit, ruach, in verse 19 is the breath of the LORD that drives the flood. The Spirit that drives out the enemy is the Spirit given to stay with the people.

typology.type: The warrior who arms Himself, verse 17
typology.fulfillment: The LORD dresses for battle in righteousness and salvation, and Isaiah 11:4-5 gives the same figure, a coming king with righteousness as the belt around His hips. The correspondence in Christ is direct: He comes as the righteous judge and the saviour in one person. Revelation 19:11 pictures Him riding in righteousness, judging and making war. Paul then lets believers wear the same pieces, Ephesians 6:14-17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8, as a gift that shares what Christ has won rather than as a self-made defence. The type falls short in one place: God wears His armour to bring justice, whereas believers wear theirs to stand firm and not to retaliate.

Moses stood in the breach, Psalm 106:23, and Ezekiel 22:30 shows God seeking such a person and finding none. The pattern is the human mediator who stands between God and the guilty. Christ fulfils it at a higher level because He is not simply a better Moses. He is the one mediator between God and men, 1 Timothy 2:5, and He always lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25. Isaiah 53:12 already said the Servant would intercede for transgressors. Moses could plead and could not remove guilt; Christ pleads on the basis of His own offering, and so what Moses could only delay He ends.

typology.type: The Redeemer who comes to Zion, verse 20
typology.fulfillment: The goel of Israel's law recovered a relative's land and person, Leviticus 25:25, and Boaz does this for Ruth, Ruth 4:9-10. The type is the kinsman who pays what the helpless cannot. In Christ, who shares our flesh and blood, Hebrews 2:14, the correspondence is literal: He is related to us by nature and redeems at the cost of Himself, Mark 10:45. Paul quotes the verse in Romans 11:26 with the promise of removal of sin. Boaz's redemption restored a family's land and name, but Christ's frees people from sin and death, and the type falls short because no earthly kinsman could free anyone from the debt of sin.

typology.type: The Spirit and words that never depart, verse 21
typology.fulfillment: The covenant promise that the Spirit and the words will stay with the people and their descendants looks ahead to the new covenant. Jeremiah 31:33 speaks of the law written on the heart, and Isaiah 44:3 of the Spirit poured on the offspring. The fulfilment comes at Pentecost, Acts 2:17-18, 38-39, where Peter says the promise is for the hearers and their children. Jesus also promises that the Helper will be with His people forever, John 14:16. The Old Testament pattern gave the Spirit to chosen leaders for a time, whereas the new covenant gives Him to every believer permanently, which is the sense of 'forevermore.'

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most plainly by what it says is missing. God looks across the whole world and sees no man who could intercede, no one righteous enough to stand in the breach. The text then does not say that He lowered the standard. It says that His own arm brought salvation and His own righteousness sustained Him, verse 16. The New Testament tells how this was done. The Son of God took our nature, so that a real human being could stand where no human had stood, and in Him the arm of the LORD became visible. John says that Isaiah saw His glory and spoke about Him, John 12:41, after quoting 'Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?' from Isaiah 53:1. Isaiah 59 is part of the same long showing of that arm.

The chapter also leads to Christ as the one who removes what Israel confessed. Verses 12 and 13 listed rebelling, denying the LORD, oppression and lies. Paul pulls verses 7 and 8 into Romans 3 to show that everyone, Jew and Gentile, is under sin, Romans 3:9-18, so that the problem of Isaiah's generation is the problem of the human race. The Redeemer of verse 20 comes to answer that problem. When Paul quotes it in Romans 11:26-27, he joins it with the words 'when I take away their sins', and ties it to the covenant of verse 21. That covenant is the one the Lord Jesus sealed at the table: 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20.

There is one more link in the garments of verse 17. The one who puts on righteousness as a breastplate later gives righteousness to others. Paul's pictures of a believer clothed with Christ, Galatians 3:27, and standing in the breastplate of righteousness, Ephesians 6:14, rest on the idea that Christ's own armour becomes the believer's protection. The cobweb clothing of verse 6, which cannot cover anyone, is replaced by a righteousness that does.

A careful reader will also note what the chapter does not claim. It does not name the Redeemer as Jesus, and it does not describe a death. The vengeance language of verse 18 sits beside the Redeemer of verse 20 in a way that fits both comings of Christ, His work for those who turn and His judgment of those who do not. The link to Christ rests on the New Testament's own use of the passage, in Romans and Ephesians and Hebrews, and not on reading hidden meanings into the garments. Where Isaiah says no one could be found, the New Testament says He was found, and that He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, Hebrews 7:25.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter says about God is a denial of two things the people might have believed. His arm is not short and His ear is not dull. Power and attentiveness are not what is in question, and a faith that blames God for the delay has misread the situation. The doctrine behind this is that God's holiness is a real moral reality, and that sin has real consequences even for people He loves. Because God is holy, sin builds barriers, and the barriers are a result of who He is and not of any failure on His part.

God is also a God who sees. In verse 15 and 16, 'The LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice' and 'He saw that there was no man.' He is not a distant spectator, and His displeasure is not coldness. It is the displeasure of one who cares for justice. In this chapter justice is not an abstract principle. It concerns the truth in the public square, the safety of those who turn from evil, and the honest pleading of cases. God's anger is aimed at the failure of care for the weak.

The central statement is that He acts alone. 'His own arm brought salvation, and His own righteousness sustained Him.' The doctrine here is the sufficiency of God. He needs no assistance and lacks nothing for the work of salvation, so that nobody can claim a share in it. At the same time it is not a cold sufficiency, because He is moved to act by what He sees. Isaiah describes the divine warrior as moved by displeasure and amazement. This is the way Scripture speaks of a God who is both unchanging in nature and truly responsive to His creatures.

Justice and mercy are held together. The same God who repays according to deeds, verse 18, sends the Redeemer to those who turn, verse 20. Wrath and rescue are not two gods. They are the same righteousness seen from two sides, and the chapter will not allow either to be dropped. He is faithful to His covenant: 'this is My covenant with them,' with a Spirit and words that never depart, verse 21. Promise is anchored in His own word, so that it does not depend on the quality of the next generation's response.

For worship, the chapter teaches two things. First, to confess without defence, as the 'we' of verses 9 to 15 does, naming sins one by one. Second, to rest in the God who has done what no one else could. Worship that begins in honest confession ends in the confidence of verse 21, that the Spirit and the word will remain with His people and their children and their children's children, because the LORD Himself has said so.

crossReferences.note: The LORD asks Moses, 'Is the LORD's arm too short?' when the people doubt He can feed them. Isaiah 59:1 uses the same idiom and answers the doubt in the same way: the arm is not short. The recall of Moses' day tells the later generation that their fear is the old fear of wilderness unbelief, now in new clothes.

Chapter 58 promised light, healing and an answer from God, 'Here I am,' if the people removed oppression and fed the hungry. Chapter 59 describes the cost of not doing so: groping in the dark and a God who does not hear. The two chapters belong together as promise and diagnosis.

God searches for a person to stand in the gap and finds no one. The wording matches Isaiah 59:16 closely. Taken together the passages show that this absence is a theme of the prophets: righteousness enough to turn away judgment could not be found in Israel.

Looks back to the time when Moses 'stood before Him in the breach' and turned aside God's wrath. It shows what an intercessor looks like when one exists, and so brings out what Isaiah 59:16 laments. The comparison also makes the later fulfilment in Christ stand out as greater than Moses.

The Servant 'made intercession for the transgressors,' using the same root as the missing intercessor of 59:16. What the people could not find in themselves, the Servant is. The two verses should be read together, since the first names the gap and the second names the person who fills it.

The warrior returns with stained garments, saying 'no one from the nations was with Me' and 'I looked, but there was no one to help.' It restates 59:16 almost word for word and shows the battle that 59:17 to 19 promised. The two chapters bracket the final section of Isaiah with one scene of lonely rescue.

Paul strings together lines from the Psalms and Isaiah to prove that all are under sin, and verses 15 to 17 lift Isaiah 59:7 and 8. In this way the confession of Isaiah's generation becomes the portrait of every generation, which is why the Redeemer is needed by Jew and Gentile alike.

Paul gives the promise of Isaiah 59:20 and 21 as the ground of Israel's future salvation, and adds 'when I take away their sins.' The quotation moves from 'to Zion' to 'from Zion', and connects the Redeemer to the covenant. The passage is the key to how the New Testament reads this chapter.

Believers are told to take up the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of salvation, the very pieces God wears in 59:17. The apostle makes it plain that the battle is against spiritual powers and not flesh and blood, so that the borrowed image changes the nature of the fight.

The new covenant promises the law written on the heart and sins remembered no more. Isaiah 59:21 promises that the Spirit and the words stay with the people for good, and the two promises describe one covenant from different sides, one inward and the other lasting through generations.

God promises to pour out His Spirit on the offspring and His blessing on the descendants. This is the earlier form of the promise in 59:21 that the Spirit will not depart from the children and grandchildren, and it shows the generational reach of the covenant as an Isaianic theme.

study.oneStory:
From the first pages of Scripture sin is a matter of separation. In Genesis 3 the pair hide from the presence of God, and cherubim with a flaming sword keep the way to the tree of life. Isaiah 59 gives the same fact in the language of building: iniquities have 'built barriers' and hidden His face. The Bible's early chapters raise the question of how a holy God and sinful people can be together, and every sacrifice, every priest and every mediator in the Old Testament is a partial answer. This chapter says the question is truly hard, because when God looked for someone able to bridge the gap He found no one.

The chapter also stands at a particular point in the Old Testament's story. The exile has been the judgment, and the return has not brought the glory the prophets spoke of. Isaiah 59 explains why, and it clears the ground for the radiance of chapter 60. The light that is withheld in 59:9 is given in 60:1, and the thing that changes in between is the arrival of the Redeemer. In the same way the wider story moves from the failure of Israel and its leaders to the coming of the Servant who succeeds where they did not.

The New Testament tells how the Redeemer came. In Christ the arm of the LORD is revealed, the intercessor appears, and the covenant of verse 21 is made in His blood. At Pentecost the Spirit comes to stay, and the words of God are put into the mouths of a new people, Jew and Gentile, who pass them to their children, Acts 2:39. Paul sees in all this the explanation of Israel's story, Romans 11, in which mercy outlasts hardening and 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable,' Romans 11:29.

The story is not finished. The vengeance of verse 18 and the fear of the name 'where the sun sets' and 'where it rises' look ahead to the day when Christ returns and every wrong is set right. The final chapters of Revelation show the end of the barrier: God dwells with His people, there is no more night, and nothing unclean can enter, Revelation 21:3 and 21:25 to 27. The people who once groped along the wall in the dark walk in a light that never fails, and the justice that stumbled in the public square is at home in a city whose gates are never shut. Isaiah 59 is therefore a hinge. It names what is wrong, tells why only God can mend it, and points to the one who does.

quiz.q: According to verses 1-2, why has salvation seemed delayed?

options.text: The people's own iniquities have built a barrier between them and God, not any weakness in His arm or ear.
options.note: Verses 1-2 explicitly rule out divine weakness and name sin as the cause.

options.text: God's power had genuinely grown too weak to save.
God had forgotten His covenant with Israel.
options.note: This voices a real, felt fear addressed elsewhere in Isaiah, but the text here names sin as the barrier, not forgetfulness on God's part.

options.text: Because Israel had not offered enough sacrifices.
options.note: The chapter's diagnosis is moral, lies and violence, not a shortfall in ritual sacrifice.

quiz.q: What does God do when He finds no one to intercede, verses 16-17?

options.text: He acts Himself, arming His own righteousness like a breastplate and salvation like a helmet.
options.note: Verses 16-17 describe God supplying what no human mediator could.
The opposite; He acts decisively to bring salvation.

options.text: He waits indefinitely for a human intercessor to appear.
options.note: This is the opposite of what happens; He does not wait, He acts immediately Himself once none is found.

options.text: He commands the people to appoint a new priest.
options.note: The text describes God's own direct action, not an institutional appointment.

quiz.q: How does Paul use Isaiah 59:20 in Romans 11:26?

options.text: He quotes it directly of the Deliverer coming from Zion, applying it to Christ's coming salvation for Israel.
He applies it only to the historical return from Babylonian exile.
options.note: This is a real, minority reading of the underlying text, but Paul's argument in Romans 11 applies it to salvation through Christ, not merely the historical return from exile.

options.text: Paul never quotes Isaiah 59 in his letters.
He uses it to argue Israel is permanently excluded from salvation.
options.note: Paul's argument is the opposite, hope for Israel's future salvation.

quiz.q: What connection does Ephesians 6 draw with this chapter's armor imagery?

options.text: Believers are told to put on the same armor of righteousness and salvation God wears here, verses 17.
options.note: Ephesians 6:14, 17 draws directly on this armor language.

options.text: Ephesians describes entirely different armor with no relation to Isaiah.
options.note: The armor pieces named, righteousness and salvation, match directly.

options.text: It applies only to literal, physical warfare against nations.
options.note: This mistakes the armor's original battle imagery for its New Testament use; Ephesians 6 explicitly reframes it as spiritual warfare, not combat between nations.

options.text: It is used to argue Christians should avoid all conflict.
options.note: The armor imagery equips believers for spiritual struggle, not passive avoidance of all conflict.

questions: The chapter says sin, not God's weakness, is what separates. What sin have you been quietly blaming on distance from God rather than owning honestly?
The confession in verses 3-15 is specific and unflinching, naming lies, violence, and injustice by name. Is your own confession this specific, or does it stay vague and general?
God was amazed that there was no one to intercede for justice. Is there a situation around you crying out for someone to stand in the gap, and could that someone be you?
God armed Himself with righteousness and salvation because no human mediator could be found. How does knowing Christ now intercedes for you change how you approach your own failures?

The chapter closes with a promise that God's Spirit and words will never depart from His people's mouths, even their children's children. What would it look like to actively pass on God's word to the next generation in your own family?

translationNotes.note: Where the sun sets, and His glory where it rises describes east to west, a merism for the whole earth fearing the LORD's name, not a claim about two separate divine glories.

Paul's quotation in Romans 11:26 follows the Greek Septuagint's rendering, the Deliverer will come out of Zion, slightly different in preposition from the Hebrew's to Zion, though the theological sense, salvation coming from and reaching Zion, is preserved either way.
